name: Chypre fragrance family

card.summary: A classic perfume family built on a citrus top, floral heart and mossy, resinous base, worn to project a polished, mature and elegant scent impression.
card.note: Traditional oakmoss is restricted in modern formulas, so contemporary chypres differ from vintage ones; fragrance allergens affect some skin.

quick.overview:
Chypre is one of the main fragrance families. It is usually described as a contrast between bright citrus (classically bergamot), a floral middle and a dry, earthy base of labdanum, oakmoss and often patchouli. The family is associated with refined, grown-up and elegant scent profiles.

For appearance and grooming, fragrance forms part of the overall impression a person makes. Practitioners pick scents by family to match the image they want to give, and chypres are often chosen for formal or mature presentation.
quick.how: People wear chypre perfumes or colognes as a finishing step in grooming, applied to skin or clothing like any fragrance. Choice is usually by family and occasion, with sampling before buying a full bottle.
quick.risks: Fragrances can cause skin irritation or allergy in some people, and oakmoss is among the regulated allergens in the industry, so modern versions are reformulated. No clinical trials concern the family as a category.

lead: Chypre is a fragrance family defined by a structure of bright citrus top notes, usually bergamot, over a base of labdanum, oakmoss and often patchouli. The name is French for Cyprus and is tied to the 1917 perfume Chypre by Francois Coty.

In grooming, scent is part of overall presentation, and people choose a family to suit the impression they want to give. Chypres are commonly associated with mature, polished and formal styles. Guerlain's Mitsouko is a standard example of the family.[1]

In Michael Edwards's widely used fragrance wheel, chypres are hard to place and would sit under parts of the Oriental and Woody families; Mitsouko falls under Mossy Woods.[1] The fragrance writer Stephen Dowthwaite links chypres with mature adults who enjoy heavy white flowers.[1]

angle.text: People use chypre fragrances as a signature scent to support a refined or formal image. The effect is on perceived presentation rather than on physical features.

infobox: Bergamot top, floral heart, labdanum / oakmoss base

paras: A chypre is built on a recognisable accord: a fresh citrus opening resolving into a dark, mossy and resinous base. Variants add fruit, leather or flowers, and are grouped as fruity, floral or leathery chypres.
Fragrance classification schemes treat chypres as a transitional group. Edwards's wheel notes that they would be located under parts of the Oriental and Woody families.[1]

Scent is discussed in grooming and style as one of the cues that shape first impressions. Chypres are generally described as formal and mature in tone, and the family is chosen by people wanting that profile.[1]
Oakmoss is a known contact allergen and is restricted by fragrance industry standards, so many modern chypres use reformulated bases. As with any fragrance, people with sensitive skin may react.

timeline.event: Francois Coty releases Chypre, giving the family its name.
Guerlain launches Mitsouko, later the family's archetype.
